newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden's TCW index given more weight - economists.
newsitem.headline: Sweden's TCW index given more weight - economists.

text.p: Economists tracking the Swedish crown are following the central bank's example and putting increasing emphasis on the Trade Currency Weighted (TCW) index as a measure of the crown and as a signal for monetary policy.
The government's TCW index, which indicates the strength of the crown against a weighted basket of currencies, is viewed increasingly by economists as an indicator for monetary policy.

"The globalisation of economies with trade taking a greater percentage of economic growth has made a lot of central banks and economists more aware of the TCW index and its importance to policy making," said PaineWebber economist James McKay.
"For an economy as open as Sweden's it does have considerable importance in terms of policy decision making and economic trends."
Nordbanken economist Erik Feldt said the TCW index was the most important measure of the crown's value.
"It has become the most important since the Riksbank began to focus on it," he told Reuters.
Although foreign exchange dealers still focus on the cross rates between the crown and the mark or the dollar, economists are following the Riksbank and concentrating on the TCW index.

The new focus followed incidents in 1994 and 1995 when moves in the TCW index were not acted upon immediately - apparently to Sweden's detriment - although signalling a necessary lift and then, cut in interest rates.
Last April, the Riksbank said between 109-118 in the TCW index was the right level for the crown's real exchange rate balance "with the emphasis on the lower half of the range."
The index is currently at 118.53 after recent weakening.
"This is a clear sign that the crown is now seen to be too weak," said economist Keld Holm of Lehman Brothers.
"We can expect the central bank to do something if this continues for a few more weeks."
Since October, the central bank has actively pursued a policy to stabilise the crown, intervening in the money market several times to support the local unit.
"The exchange rate is one of the many important indicators for future price development," Claes Berg, chief economist at the Riksbank, told Reuters.
Sweden's monetary policy is based on price stability with a target of two percent inflation, with flexibility to move one percentage point in either direction.

As the central bank intervened, economists said market participants could interpret that the bank had a certain target for the crown against the mark or dollar, but it could be that moves in the TCW index were prompting the action.
"I suspect they are targeting the TCW because it is economically more viable," said one economist.
McKay said Sweden's determination to keep the crown stable coincided with its reluctance to join Europe's Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) as public opinion was running firmly against such a move.

"The Riksbank is trying to pursue a policy where it can turn around and say it has got a stable exchange rate without being linked to the Exchange Rate Mechanism and so still meet the criteria to join the EMU," he said.
Holm said: "(Maintaining this stabiity) is like a substitute for euro membership, and key to membership of EMU."
